Section 1
The Twitter feud between Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt and actor Ralf Little began innocuously enough. On a Sunday morning in late autumn, Hunt appeared on The Andrew Marr Show, confidently declaring that under his watch, the NHS had delivered "the biggest expansion of mental health provision in Europe." It was a bold claim, delivered with the practiced ease of a seasoned politician. Watching from his London flat, Ralf Little, the actor beloved for his role as the laid-back Anthony in The Royle Family, felt his blood pressure rising. Having lost a close friend to suicide just months earlier, mental health provision was a subject close to his heart. Unable to contain his frustration, he grabbed his phone and fired off a tweet that would ignite an unprecedented political firestorm: "Jeremy Hunt is knowingly lying to the public about mental health statistics. Sue me if I'm wrong."

Section 2
Hunt's initial silence spoke volumes. For a week, political commentators speculated whether the Health Secretary would respond to such a direct challenge from a celebrity. When Hunt finally broke his silence, it was with characteristic political bluster. He "double dared" Little to prove his claims, accompanying his challenge with a barrage of statistics that he claimed vindicated his position. But Little, who had spent the intervening week researching with the dedication of an investigative journalist, was ready. What followed was a masterclass in social media activism: over 40 meticulously researched tweets, each one systematically dismantling Hunt's arguments with data from Full Fact, the UK's independent fact-checking charity. The thread went viral, shared over 15,000 times within hours, as mental health professionals, patients, and advocates rallied behind the actor's cause.

Section 3
The public nature of the dispute exposed deep fissures in the government's mental health narrative. Hunt's claim about 30,000 new mental health workers had already been embarrassingly corrected in Parliament – the actual figure was just 692, a discrepancy of 43 times. Now, faced with Little's relentless fact-checking, Hunt found himself in the unusual position of having to justify his statistics tweet by tweet. His Monday response, a sprawling 26-tweet thread that lost its chronological order midway through, only served to highlight his discomfort. "Now I know you are a funny bloke," Hunt wrote, attempting to strike a conciliatory tone while simultaneously defending his position. He cited an increase in mental health nurse training places and quoted from a New York Times article – apparently unaware that the article had been corrected three times after challenges from former shadow minister for mental health, Luciana Berger.

Section 4
Behind the Twitter drama lay a more serious crisis. Mental health services across the UK were stretched to breaking point, with patients facing months-long waiting lists and chronic staff shortages. Little's intervention had given voice to thousands who felt betrayed by government promises. Mental health charities reported a surge in engagement as the debate raged on, with professionals using the hashtag #LittleVsHunt to share their own experiences of an underfunded system. One psychiatric nurse from Manchester tweeted: "I've worked in mental health for 15 years. We're not seeing expansion – we're watching a slow collapse." The Royal College of Psychiatrists issued a measured statement acknowledging the "productive debate" while calling for "urgent action rather than rhetoric" on mental health funding.

Section 5
As the Twitter war entered its third week, it had transformed from a celebrity spat into a national conversation about political accountability and mental health care. Little, initially dismissed by some commentators as an actor out of his depth, had proven himself a formidable opponent armed with facts and moral conviction. Hunt, meanwhile, faced increasing pressure to provide concrete evidence for his claims. The incident raised profound questions about how health policy is communicated in the age of social media, where a comedian could effectively fact-check a cabinet minister in real-time before an audience of millions. Political analysts noted that this represented a new form of democratic accountability, where traditional gatekeepers of information could be bypassed entirely. As one commentator observed: "Ralf Little has done more to scrutinize government mental health policy in three weeks than some parliamentary committees manage in months." The Health Secretary's office announced that Hunt would be making a detailed statement on mental health funding in the Commons, a clear indication that the Twitter row had forced a policy reckoning at the highest levels of government.
